Linking numbers in three-manifolds

Patricia Cahn and Alexandra Kjuchukova
Abstract.

Let MM be a connected, closed, oriented three-manifold and KK, LL two rationally null-homologous oriented simple closed curves in MM. We give an explicit algorithm for computing the linking number between KK and LL in terms of a presentation of MM as an irregular dihedral 33-fold cover of S3S^{3} branched along a knot α⊂S3\alpha\subset S^{3}. Since every closed, oriented three-manifold admits such a presentation, our results apply to all (well-defined) linking numbers in all three-manifolds. Furthermore, ribbon obstructions for a knot α\alpha can be derived from dihedral covers of α\alpha. The linking numbers we compute are necessary for evaluating one such obstruction. This work is a step toward testing potential counter-examples to the Slice-Ribbon Conjecture, among other applications.

1. Introduction

The notion of linking number between knots in S3S^{3} dates back at least as far as Gauss [13]. More generally, given a closed, oriented three-manifold MM and two rationally null-homologous, oriented, simple closed curves K,L⊂MK,L\subset M, the linking number l​k​(K,L)lk(K,L) is defined as well. It is given by 1n​(K⋅CL)\dfrac{1}{n}\left(K\cdot C_{L}\right), where CLC_{L} is a 2-chain in MM with boundary n​LnL, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and ⋅\cdot denotes the signed intersection number. This linking number is well-defined and symmetric [3].

Let the three-manifold MM be presented as a 3-fold irregular dihedral branched cover of S3S^{3}, branched along a knot. Every closed oriented three-manifold admits such a presentation [16, 17, 21]. Consider a branched cover f:M→S3f:M\to S^{3} of this type, and let γ,δ⊂S3\gamma,\delta\subset S^{3} be oriented, closed curves embedded disjointly from each other and from the branching set α\alpha of ff. In Theorem 2, we give a formula for the linking number in MM between any two connected components of the pre-images of γ\gamma and δ\delta, in the case where the pre-images of γ\gamma and δ\delta have three connected compents each. The general case is given in Section 4.1. This linking number is computed in terms of a diagram of the link α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta. The geometric construction underlying the computation is reviewed in Section 1.1 and serves to complement the theorem statement, which is combinatorial in flavor. Linking numbers in dihedral branched covers of S3S^{3} are needed for calculating several knot and three-manifold invariants [20, 8, 19, 14]; applications are considered in Section 1.2.

Briefly, our technique is the following. The cone on the link α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta gives a cell structure on S3S^{3} which lifts, via the map ff, to a cell structure on MM. Two-chains bounding closed connected components of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) and f−1​(δ)f^{-1}(\delta) are found by solving a system of linear equations. We obtain these equations by examining the diagram of α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta used to construct the cell structure on MM. Finally, intersection numbers between lifts of δ\delta and the 2-chains bounding lifts of γ\gamma are computed from local data about the relevant 1- and 2-cells.

Classically, a knot invariant is derived from linking numbers in branched covers as follows. Let α⊂S3\alpha\subset S^{3} be a Fox 33-colorable knot. Any 3-coloring of α\alpha determines an irregular dihedral 33-fold covering map f:M→S3f:M\to S^{3} with branching set α\alpha, as reviewed in Section 2.1. Given such a three-fold cover ff, the preimage of the branching set, f−1​(α)f^{-1}(\alpha), has two connected components whose linking number, in MM, is either a rational number or undefined. The set of these linking numbers over all distinct 3-colorings of α\alpha is called the linking number invariant of α\alpha. Analogous invariants can be derived for more general Fox pp-colorings and other types of branched covers.

Dihedral linking numbers have been instrumental in distinguishing and tabulating knots, including in various situations where other invariants do not suffice. The linking number invariant was introduced by Reidemeister in [26], where he applied it to tell apart two knots with the same Alexander polynomial. In [27], Riley generalized this idea and used linking numbers in 5-fold (non-dihedral) branched covers to distinguish a pair of mutants whose Alexander polynomials were trivial. Two 36-crossing knots with the same Jones polynomial were distinguished by Birman using linking numbers in four-fold simple branched covers [2].

Linking numbers in dihedral branched covers are also good for studying certain properties of knots: they provide an obstruction to amphichirality [12, 24] and invertibility [15]. But the most well-known story is perhaps that of the Perko Pair, which consists of “two” knots which dihedral linking numbers failed to distinguish. These knots turned out to be isotopic, and constituted an accidental duplicate in Conway’s knot table [10]. The mistake was corrected by Perko. His discovery also provided a counterexample to a conjecture of Tait – stating that two reduced alternating diagrams of a given knot have equal the writhe – previously believed to be established as a theorem.

Historically, efforts at knot classification have relied heavily on linking numbers in branched covers. Bankwitz and Schumann [1] classified knots of up to nine crossings using linking numbers in dihedral covers of 2-bridge knots as their primary tool. (Note that the irregular dihedral branched cover of a 2-bridge knot is always S3S^{3}; a proof of this old observation is recalled in [18].) Perko extended these methods, which allowed him to complete the classification to knots of ten and eleven crossings [24]. Burde proved that dihedral linking numbers can tell apart all 2-bridge knots [4], without regard to crossing number. The largest-scale computation of linking numbers was done by Dowker and Thistlethwaite, who succeeded in tabulating millions of knots [11]. It is difficult to imagine that today’s knot tables would be as advanced in the absence of Reidemeister’s extremely powerful idea to consider linking numbers between the branch curves in non-cyclic branched covers of knots. For a more detailed account of the role of linking numbers in knot theory, as well as several illuminating examples, see [25].

Our results extend the classical linking number computation to include linking numbers of curves other than the branch curves, namely, closed connected components of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) and f−1​(δ)f^{-1}(\delta), where γ,δ⊂S3\gamma,\delta\subset S^{3} are curves in the complement of the branching set. It is helpful to formally regard points on γ\gamma and δ\delta as points on the branching set of ff, with the property that each of their pre-images has branching index 1. Accordingly, we refer to γ\gamma and δ\delta as a pseudo-branch curves of ff. We will call each closed connected component of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) (resp. f−1​(δ)f^{-1}(\delta)) a lift of γ\gamma (resp. δ\delta). Finally, despite the apparent ambiguity, we will also use the phrase “pseudo-branch curves” to refer to the lifts themselves. Since every closed, connected, oriented 3-manifold admits a presentation as a 3-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3} branched along a knot, our methods compute all well-defined linking numbers in all 3-manifolds; this is proved at the end of Section 1.1.

1.1. Algorithm overview and the main theorem

We now summarize the geometric setup underlying our computation, and state our main theorem. Let α⊂S3\alpha\subset S^{3} be a 3-colored knot and f:M→S3f:M\to S^{3} be the corresponding dihedral cover of S3S^{3} branched along α\alpha. Let γ\gamma, δ⊂S3−α\delta\subset S^{3}-\alpha be two disjoint, oriented knots. We treat the homomorphism ρ:π1​(S3−α)↠D3\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha)\twoheadrightarrow D_{3} from which the branched cover ff arises as a homomorphism of π1​(S3−α−γ−δ)\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha-\gamma-\delta) in which meridians of γ\gamma and δ\delta all map to the trivial element; accordingly, we refer to γ\gamma, δ\delta as pseudo-branch curves. We compute linking numbers between connected components of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) and f−1​(δ)f^{-1}(\delta) by the following procedure.

  1. (1)

    Choose a cell structure on S3S^{3} determined by the cone on the link α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta; see Figure 2.

  2. (2)

    Lift this cell structure to MM by examining the lifts of the cells near each crossing of the link diagram downstairs; see, for example, Figure 7. This cell structure contains the lifts of the pseudo-branch curves as 1-subcomplexes.

  3. (3)

    Solve a linear system to determine which of the lifts of the pseudo-branch curves are rationally null-homologous. For each rationally null-homologous lift of a pseudo-branch curve, we find an explicit 2-chain which it bounds.

  4. (4)

    For each pair of rationally null-homologous lifts of the pseudo-branch curves, we compute linking numbers by adding up the signed intersection numbers of the relevant 1- and 2-cells.

Steps (1) and (2) are discussed in Section 2. Step (3) is carried out in Proposition 1, which determines when a lift of a pseudo-branch curve bounds a 2-chain, and finds the 2-chain when it exists. Step (4) is the content of Theorem 2, which gives a formula for the linking number between lifts of pseudo-branch curves.

We now state our main results, Proposition 1 and Theorem 2. We assume for the moment that each of the pseudo-branch curves has three (closed, connected) lifts, and denote these by γj\gamma_{j} and δk\delta_{k}, j,k∈{1,2,3}j,k\in\{1,2,3\}. Both γj\gamma_{j} and δk\delta_{k} must be rationally null-homologous for their linking number to be well-defined. We verify this condition by reversing the roles of γ\gamma and δ\delta in our computations and thus making sure that each of the curves bounds a 2-chain. The lift γj\gamma_{j} is rationally null-homologous if and only if a solution (x0j,x1j,…,xm−1j)∈ℚm(x_{0}^{j},x_{1}^{j},\dots,x_{m-1}^{j})\in\mathbb{Q}^{m} to the system of equations in Proposition 1 exists. The xijx^{j}_{i} describe a rational 2-chain with boundary γj\gamma_{j}, namely they are coefficients for the 2-cells A2,iA_{2,i} and −A3,i-A_{3,i} in the chain (these 2-cells are defined in Section 2.3). Additional notation is given in Table 1. The precise definitions of items 10 to 14 in the table are technical and given in the equations listed, which can be found in Sections 2.2 and 4.2.

Theorem 2.

Let f:M→S3f:M\to S^{3} be a three-fold irregular dihedral cover branched along a knot α\alpha, and let γ,δ⊂S3−α\gamma,\delta\subset S^{3}-\alpha. If the lifts γj\gamma_{j} and δk\delta_{k} are rationally null-homologous closed loops in MM for j,k∈{1,2,3}j,k\in\{1,2,3\}, then the linking number Ij,kI_{j,k} of γj\gamma_{j} with δk\delta_{k} is the sum:

Ij,k=∑i=0t−1ci,I_{j,k}=\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}c_{i},

where cic_{i} is given by

ci={ϵ5k​(i)​xf⁡(i)jif ​hi​ terminates at an arc ​kf⁡(i)​ of ​α;ϵδ​(i)​ϵ6j,k​(i)if ​hi​ terminates at an arc of ​γ;0if ​hi​ terminates at an arc of ​δ.c_{i}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\epsilon_{5}^{k}(i)x^{j}_{f(i)}&\text{if }h_{i}\text{ terminates at an arc }k_{f(i)}\text{ of }\alpha;\\ \epsilon_{\delta}(i)\epsilon_{6}^{j,k}(i)&\text{if }h_{i}\text{ terminates at an arc of }\gamma;\\ 0&\text{if }h_{i}\text{ terminates at an arc of }\delta.\\ \end{array}\right.

We have focused here on the case where each pseudo-branch curve lifts to three closed loops because this case is the one we encounter exclusively in our main application [6]. In general, the number of connected components of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) is determined by the image of [γ]∈π1​(S3−α)[\gamma]\in\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha) under the homomorphism π1​(S3−α)→D3\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha)\to D_{3} which determines the branched cover ff. Therefore, the number of components of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) can be determined from the the link diagram α∪γ\alpha\cup\gamma where α\alpha is 3-colored. Computations involving pseudo-branch curves whose pre-images under the branched covering map consist of fewer than three connected components can be carried out using the same techniques; see Section 4.1. Theorem 2 can also be used to compute linking numbers between the branch curves themselves, as well as linking numbers between branch and pseudo-branch curves, as discussed in Sections 4.2 and 4.3.

Our methods compute all well-defined linking numbers in all closed, connected, oriented 3-manifolds.

Lemma 3.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented 3-manifold, and let K∪LK\cup L be a 2-component oriented link in MM. Denote by f:M→S3f:M\rightarrow S^{3} a 3-fold irregular dihedral cover whose branching set is the knot α⊂S3\alpha\subset S^{3}. Then K∪LK\cup L is isotopic to a link K′∪L′K^{\prime}\cup L^{\prime} such that f⁡(K′∪L′)f(K^{\prime}\cup L^{\prime}) is a link disjoint from α\alpha.

This lemma follows from a standard general position argument. See, for example, [22], in which the authors give a diagrammatic theory for links in 3-manifolds represented as 3-fold covers of S3S^{3}. In particular, their labelled Reidemeister moves provide an alternative approach to computing linking numbers between lifts of pseudo-branch curves.

Given rationally null-homologous KK, LL as in the above lemma, note that l​k​(K,L)=l​k​(K′,L′)lk(K,L)=lk(K^{\prime},L^{\prime}), since the two links (K,L)(K,L) and (K′,L′)(K^{\prime},L^{\prime}) are isotopic. Now let γ=f⁡(K′)\gamma=f(K^{\prime}) and δ=f⁡(L′)\delta=f(L^{\prime}). That is, K′K^{\prime} and L′L^{\prime} are closed connected components of f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) and f−1​(δ)f^{-1}(\delta), respectively. In the language of this paper, f−1​(γ)f^{-1}(\gamma) and f−1​(δ)f^{-1}(\delta) are lifts of the pseudo-branch curves γ\gamma and δ\delta. If γ\gamma and δ\delta each have three lifts, the linking number of K′K^{\prime} and L′L^{\prime} can be computed by the formula given in Theorem 2, yielding the linking number of KK and LL. Otherwise the linking number can be computed as in Section 4.1.

1.2. Applications to branched covers of 4-manifolds and the Slice-Ribbon Conjecture.

In [8], Cappell and Shaneson gave a formula, in terms of linking numbers of lifts of pseudo-branch curves, for the Rokhlin μ\mu invariant of a dihedral cover of knot α\alpha. As noted earlier, every oriented three-manifold is a dihedral cover of a knot [16, 17, 21]; hence, this method is universal. Secondly, Litherland [20] showed that Casson-Gordon invariants of a knot can also be computed using linking numbers of pseudo-branch curves in a branched cover. The algorithm provided herein allows for the execution of a key missing step in evaluating Casson-Gordon and Rokhlin μ\mu invariants via the above methods.

The application we focus on is the computation of a ribbon obstruction Ξp\Xi_{p} arising in the study of singular dihedral branched covers of four-manifolds. In [18], the second author gives a formula for the signature of a pp-fold irregular dihedral branched cover f:Y→Xf:Y\to X between closed oriented topological four-manifolds XX and YY, in the case where the branching set BB of ff is a closed oriented surface embedded in the base XX with a cone singularity described by a knot α⊂S3\alpha\subset S^{3}. This formula shows that the signature of YY deviates from the locally flat case by a defect term, Ξp​(α)\Xi_{p}(\alpha), which is determined by the singularity α\alpha. The term Ξp​(α)\Xi_{p}(\alpha) can be calculated in part via linking numbers of pseudo-branch curves in a dihedral cover of α\alpha. If the base XX of the covering map ff is in fact S4S^{4}, the signature of the cover YY is exactly equal to Ξp​(α)\Xi_{p}(\alpha). In particular, our method for computing linking numbers between pseudo-branch curves allows us to determine the signature of a dihedral branched cover of S4S^{4} in terms of combinatorial data about the singularity on the branching set. We give an example of such a computation, using the algorithm given in this paper, in [6]. Furthermore, for a slice knot α\alpha, the integer Ξp​(α)\Xi_{p}(\alpha) can be used to derive an obstruction to α\alpha being homotopy ribbon [5, 14]. Precisely, for a fixed pp, Ξp​(α)\Xi_{p}(\alpha) is constrained in a fixed range for all homotopy ribbon knots. This obstruction provides a new method to test counter-examples to the Slice-Ribbon conjecture. We are interested in applying the results of this paper to search for a slice knot which is not ribbon; we use our algorithm to compute Ξ3\Xi_{3} for concrete examples of slice knots in [6]. In [7] we give an infinite family of knots whose four-genus is computed with the help of the Ξ3\Xi_{3} invariant. An effective method for evaluating linking numbers in three-manifolds is essential for using the Ξp​(α)\Xi_{p}(\alpha) invariant to study knot four-genus and knot concordance.

1.3. Overview of the article.

In Section 2, we recall the definition of an irregular dihedral cover, and we discuss the relevant cell structure on S3S^{3}, as well its lift to the cover MM. In Section 3 we construct the rational 2-chains bounding the pseudo-branch curves, proving Proposition 1. In Section 4, we prove Theorem 2, which gives the formula for the linking numbers between lifts of pseudo-branch curves, as well as Theorem 5, which gives an analogous formula for the linking numbers between lifts of a pseudo-branch curve and a branch curve. Section 5 illustrates our algorithm on a concrete example of a three-fold dihedral cover and several pseudo-branch curves therein. Due to the large number of cells used, computations by hand quickly evolve into an unwieldy task, even for the most resolute and concentrated persons. Our algorithm for calculating linking numbers in branched covers has therefore been implemented in Python. The code is included in the Appendix11 1 Appendix not included in the published version..

2. A combinatorial method for computing linking numbers

2.1. Irregular dihedral covers

Let α\alpha be a knot in S3S^{3} and f:M→S3f:M\to S^{3} a covering map branched along α\alpha. The branched cover ff is determined by its unbranched counterpart, f|f−1(S3−α)f_{|f^{-1}(S^{3}-\alpha)}. Thus, we can associate to it a group homomorphism ρ:π1​(S3−α)→G\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha)\rightarrow G for some group GG. For us, GG is always DpD_{p}, the dihedral group of order 2​p2p, ρ\rho is surjective, and pp is odd. The homomorphism ρ\rho induces the regular 2​p2p-fold dihedral cover of (S3,α)(S^{3},\alpha); this cover corresponds to the subgroup ker⁡ρ⊂π1​(S3−α)\ker\rho\subset\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha). The irregular pp-fold dihedral cover of (S3,α)(S^{3},\alpha), also induced by ρ\rho, corresponds to a subgroup ρ−1​(ℤ2)⊂π1​(S3−α)\rho^{-1}(\mathbb{Z}_{2})\subset\pi_{1}(S^{3}-\alpha), where ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} can be any subgroup of DpD_{p} of order 2. The irregular dihedral cover is a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quotient of the regular one, and different choices of subgroup ℤ2⊂Dp\mathbb{Z}_{2}\subset D_{p} correspond to different choices of an involution. Recall also that ρ\rho can be represented by a pp-coloring of the knot diagram, where the “color” of each arc indicates the element in DpD_{p} of order 2 to which ρ\rho maps the element of the knot group corresponding to the meridian of this arc. In this paper we focus on 3-fold irregular dihedral covers. The colors 1, 2, and 3 correspond to the transpositions (23)(23), (13)(13), and (12)(12) respectively. Given a 3-fold dihedral cover, the pre-image of the knot α\alpha has two connected components α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, with branching indices 1 and 2 respectively.

2.2. The cell structure on S3S^{3}

This section serves primarily to describe the cell structure on S3S^{3} determined by the cone on the link α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta, and some related notation. This is a subdivision of the cell structure used by Perko [23] to compute the linking number of the branch curves α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}.

We begin by focusing on the part of the cell structure determined only by the cone on α∪γ\alpha\cup\gamma, as the lifts of these 2-cells are sufficient to construct a 2-chain bounding each lift of γ\gamma. The relevant notation is summarized in Table 1.

The arcs of α\alpha in the link diagram of α∪γ\alpha\cup\gamma are labelled k0k_{0}, k1k_{1}, …\dots, km−1k_{m-1}, proceeding along the diagram in the direction of the orientation of α\alpha; mm is the sum of the number of crossings of α\alpha with itself and the number of crossings of α\alpha with γ\gamma where α\alpha passes under γ\gamma. For the purposes of labeling the lifts of 2-cells in a systematic way, we require that the diagram of α\alpha have an even number of crossings. We can arrange this to be the case by performing a Type 1 Reidemeister move on α\alpha, if necessary. From now on, we assume without further comment that the diagram of α\alpha has this property. Similarly, the arcs of γ\gamma are labelled g0g_{0}, g1g_{1}, …\dots, gs−1g_{s-1}, where ss is the number of crossings of γ\gamma with itself plus the number of crossings of α\alpha with γ\gamma where γ\gamma passes under α\alpha. We refer to the crossing at the head of arc kik_{i} as the it​hi^{th} crossing of α\alpha, and the crossing at the head of the arc gig_{i} as the it​hi^{th} crossing of γ\gamma; in each case the over-arc could be an arc of α\alpha or γ\gamma. After the arcs kik_{i} and gig_{i} have been labelled, we introduce the third link component δ\delta to the diagram, and label its arcs h0h_{0}, h1h_{1}, …\dots, ht−1h_{t-1}. If several consecutive arcs of δ\delta are separated by over-arcs of δ\delta, we treat these arcs as a single long arc with one label hih_{i}, so tt above is the number of crossings of δ\delta under α\alpha plus the number of crossings of δ\delta under γ\gamma (this allows us to slightly simplify the input to the computer program).

We denote by ϵ⁡(i)\epsilon(i), ϵγ​(i)\epsilon_{\gamma}(i), or ϵδ​(i)\epsilon_{\delta}(i) the local writhe number at the head of kik_{i}, gig_{i}, or hih_{i} respectively.

The cell structure on S3S^{3}, pictured in Figure 2, consists of:

  1. (1)

    One 00-cell, which is the cone point of the cone on the link α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta.

  2. (2)

    One “horizontal”11-cell for each arc in the link diagram: these are the kik_{i}, gig_{i}, and hih_{i}.

  3. (3)

    One “vertical” 11-cell for each crossing in the link diagram. The vertical 1-cell connecting the head of an arc of kik_{i} or gig_{i} to the 00-cell is denoted aia_{i} or bib_{i}, respectively.

  4. (4)

    One “vertical” 22-cell for each crossing in the link diagram. The vertical 2-cell below an arc kik_{i} or gig_{i} is denoted AiA_{i} or BiB_{i}, respectively.

  5. (5)

    One 3-cell, e3e^{3}, which is the complement of the cone on the link.

Note that ∂Ai=ki+ai−ai−1\partial A_{i}=k_{i}+a_{i}-a_{i-1}, and ∂Bi=gi+bi−bi−1\partial B_{i}=g_{i}+b_{i}-b_{i-1}.

Denote by c⁡(i)c(i) the color, 1, 2, or 3, assigned to the arc kik_{i}. Let f⁡(i)f(i) denote the subscript jj of the arc kjk_{j} or gjg_{j} which passes over crossing ii of α\alpha, and let fγ​(i)f_{\gamma}(i) denote the subscript jj of the arc (kjk_{j} or gjg_{j}) passing over crossing ii of γ\gamma; fδ​(i)f_{\delta}(i) is defined similarly. For example, in Figure 2, f⁡(3)=7f(3)=7, fγ​(0)=5f_{\gamma}(0)=5, fγ​(1)=6f_{\gamma}(1)=6, and fδ​(0)=4f_{\delta}(0)=4. 2.3. The cell structure on MM

Now we describe how to lift our cell structure to MM and introduce notation for the lifts of the cells. Our strategy is to understand the lift of the cell structure on S3S^{3} in a neighborhood of each crossing, and label the cells near the lift of each crossing in a systematic way. For example, Figure 5 shows the cells near a self-crossing of α\alpha in S3S^{3}. Figure 7 shows one way these cells lift if the crossing is inhomogenous, that is, the colors on the three arcs are all different. In contrast, Figure 9 shows one way these cells lift if the crossing is homogeneous, that is, the three colors on the arcs are the same. Later in this section we explain how these figures are constructed, what the possible configurations of cells above a crossing are, and how to determine which configuration arises. We must also analyze the lifts of cells near self-crossings of γ\gamma, and near crossings of α\alpha under γ\gamma. We adopt some of the notation of [23] for the lifts of cells coming from the knot α\alpha. We introduce a new way of visualizing the cell structure which simplifies the task of computing linking numbers between pseudo-branch curves, and generalizes easily to the case where α\alpha is Fox pp-colored for p≥5.p\geq 5.

Let α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} denote the index-1 and index-2 branch curves in MM of the 3-fold irregular branched covering map f:M→S3f:M\rightarrow S^{3}; note α1∪α2=f−1​(α)\alpha_{1}\cup\alpha_{2}=f^{-1}(\alpha). 4. Computing linking numbers and proof of Theorem 2

To complete the computation, we introduce the second pseudo-branch curve δ\delta into the diagram α∪γ\alpha\cup\gamma without changing the subscripts on the arcs kik_{i} of α\alpha or the arcs gig_{i} of γ\gamma. We label the arcs of δ\delta by h0,…,ht−1h_{0},\dots,h_{t-1}, where tt is the number of crossings of δ\delta under α\alpha plus the number of crossings of δ\delta under γ\gamma. (Self-crossings of δ\delta do not contribute anything to the linking number. When numbering arcs of δ\delta for the computer program, we will assign consecutive arcs of δ\delta the same number if they are separated by an overcrossing by another arc of δ\delta, in order to slightly simplify the input.)

We again use the notation fδ​(i)f_{\delta}(i), or just f⁡(i)f(i), to denote the subscript of the overstrand at the head of the arc hih_{i}. As was the case with γ\gamma, the preimage of the curve δ\delta may have one, two or three connected components. We begin with the case where the preimages of both γ\gamma and δ\delta are three closed loops. Let δ1\delta_{1}, δ2\delta_{2}, and δ3\delta_{3} denote the three lifts of δ\delta; as before, we choose the subscripts on the δk\delta_{k} so that the lift of h0h_{0} which is contained in the 3-cell ek3e^{3}_{k} is a subset of δk\delta_{k}. Let hk,ih_{k,i} denote the lift of hih_{i} which is a subset of δk\delta_{k}. Let lkh​(i)l^{h}_{k}(i) denote the subscript ss of the 3-cell es3e^{3}_{s} which contains the arc hk,ih_{k,i}. We now compute the linking number Ij,kI_{j,k} of γj\gamma_{j} with δk\delta_{k}, which amounts to proving our main theorem.

Theorem 2.

Let f:M→S3f:M\to S^{3} be a three-fold irregular dihedral cover branched along a knot α\alpha, and let γ,δ⊂S3−α\gamma,\delta\subset S^{3}-\alpha. If the lifts γj\gamma_{j} and δk\delta_{k} are rationally null-homologous closed loops in MM for j,k∈{1,2,3}j,k\in\{1,2,3\}, then the linking number Ij,kI_{j,k} of γj\gamma_{j} with δk\delta_{k} is the sum:

4.1. A note on pseudo-branch curves which lift to fewer than 3 loops

The pre-image of a pseudo-branch curve γ\gamma under the covering map may well have fewer than three connected components. Precisely, the lifts of γ\gamma could include two closed loops γ1⋅γ2\gamma_{1}\cdot\gamma_{2} and γ3\gamma_{3}, or one closed loop γ1⋅γ2⋅γ3\gamma_{1}\cdot\gamma_{2}\cdot\gamma_{3}, where each γj\gamma_{j} covers γ\gamma and ⋅\cdot denotes concatenation of paths.

If some concatenation σ\sigma of the γi\gamma_{i}’s forms a closed, rationally null-homologous loop, we can still find a 2-chain CσC_{\sigma} with boundary σ\sigma using the methods given in the previous Section 3 . We do this by writing down the three systems of equations for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3 listed in Proposition 1. The 2-chain CσC_{\sigma} bounding σ\sigma is then:

Cσ=∑j∈S(∑i=0s−1Bj,i+∑i=0m−1xij​(A2,i−A3,i)).C_{\sigma}=\sum_{j\in S}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}B_{j,i}+\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}x_{i}^{j}(A_{2,i}-A_{3,i})\right).

Now let’s consider the linking number between two such pseudo-branch curves. Suppose the closed loop σ\sigma is a concatenation of paths γi\gamma_{i}, where i∈S⊂{1,2,3}i\in S\subset\{1,2,3\}, and the closed loop τ\tau is a concatenation of paths δi\delta_{i}, where i∈T⊂{1,2,3}i\in T\subset\{1,2,3\} and each δi\delta_{i} is a lift of a second pseudo-branch curve δ⊂S3−α\delta\subset S^{3}-\alpha. It follows from Section 4.1 that, in the notation of the same section, if σ\sigma and τ\tau are rationally null-homologous, their linking number is equal to ∑j∈S,k∈TIj,k.\sum_{j\in S,k\in T}I_{j,k}.

4.2. Linking numbers between branch curves

Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 also allow us to compute linking number of the branch cuves α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, as follows.

Let the pseudo-branch curve γ\gamma be a push-off of α\alpha along the vector field A→\vec{A} from Section 2.3. Since the diagram of α\alpha has an even number of crossings, γ\gamma has three lifts. Two are isotopic to the index-2 lift of α\alpha (these are push-offs of α2\alpha_{2} along ±A→2\pm\vec{A}_{2}), and one is isotopic to the index-1 lift of α\alpha. Now take a second push-off δ\delta of α\alpha along A→\vec{A}, disjoint from γ\gamma. Theorem 2 applied to a diagram of the link α∪γ∪δ\alpha\cup\gamma\cup\delta gives the linking number of α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}.

From this point of view, our results generalize the result of Perko [23], which gives an algorithm for computing the linking number of α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} using a cell structure determined by the cone on α\alpha. Recall the cell structure we introduce in Section 2.3 is a subdivision of Perko’s cell structure.

5. Examples

To conclude, we illustrate the output of the algorithm on a collection of pseudo-branch curves. The branch curve α\alpha is a connected sum of two 3-colored trefoil knots. Since the trefoil is a 2-bridge knot, its irregular 3-fold dihedral cover is again S3S^{3}. From there, one can check that the irregular 3-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3} branched along the connected sum α\alpha is S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2}.

Now we choose pseudo-branch curves on which to perform our computations. We choose curves which appear in our primary applications—see Section 1.2. We briefly explain the context here, though it is not necessary for understanding the linking number computation itself.

5.1. Characteristic knots

Cappell and Shaneson proved in [9] that the regular and irregular pp-fold dihedral covers of (S3,α)(S^{3},\alpha) can be constructed from a pp-fold cyclic cover of S3S^{3} branched along an associated knot β⊂S3−α\beta\subset S^{3}-\alpha, which they called a mod pp characteristic knot for α\alpha. They also showed that mod pp characteristic knots for α\alpha, up to equivalence, are in one-to-one correspondence with pp-fold irregular dihedral covers of α\alpha. For a precise definition, let VV be a Seifert surface for α\alpha and LVL_{V} the corresponding linking form. A knot β⊂V∘\beta\subset V^{\circ} is a mod pp characteristic knot for α\alpha if [β][\beta] is primitive in H1​(V,ℤ)H_{1}(V;\mathbb{Z}) and (LV+LVT)​β≡0modp(L_{V}+L_{V}^{T})\beta\equiv 0\mod p.

The characteristic knots of α\alpha play an essential role in many of the potential applications of this work, including the computation of Casson-Gordon invariants [20], the Rokhlin μ\mu invariant [9], and the computation of the invariant Ξp\Xi_{p} discussed earlier [19, 6]. Specifically, these invariants are computed using linking numbers of lifts of curves in V−βV-\beta, where VV is a Seifert surface for α\alpha, and β\beta is a characteristic knot. For the purposes of this paper, the essential property of a mod 3 characteristic knot β⊂V\beta\subset V is that every simple closed curve in V−βV-\beta lifts to three closed curves in the dihedral cover of α\alpha corresponding to β\beta. As a result, we have focused on computations with curves in S3−αS^{3}-\alpha whose lifts to a three-fold dihedral cover of (S3,α)(S^{3},\alpha) have three connected components.

In the examples below, we let VV be the connected sum of two copies of the familiar Seifert surface for the minimal-crossing diagram of the trefoil in 2-bridge position, namely a surface consisting of two disks joined by three twisted bands. The characteristic knot β\beta is then the connected sum of two copies of a characteristic knot for the trefoil; it is shown in blue in Figures 16 and 17.

5.2. Examples

We apply our algorithm to the following pseudo-branch curves: the characteristic knot β\beta, defined above; an essential curve ω1\omega_{1} (see Figure 16) in V−βV-\beta, which has one null-homologous lift and two homologically nontrivial lifts; and a pseudo-branch curve ω2\omega_{2} (see Figure 17) which is a push-off of a curve in VV intersecting β\beta once transversely, and lifts to a single null-homologous closed curve.

Our computer algorithm detects the number of lifts and whether each is rationally null-homologous, and allows us to compute the linking numbers of all pairs of rationally null-homologous lifts. The results of this computation are discussed below. In each part, we choose one of the curves above to play the role of the first pseudo-branch curve, referred to as γ\gamma throughout the previous sections (this is the curve for which we find bounding 2-chains), and then compute linking numbers by letting the other curves play the role of the second pseudo-branch curve δ\delta.

Part I. To start, the role of the first pseudo-branch curve, denoted by γ\gamma throughout the previous sections, is played by the characteristic knot β.\beta.

We include all the input needed for the computer program for our first computation, which finds intersection numbers of lifts of ω1\omega_{1} with 2-chains whose boundaries are lifts of β\beta. The input for other computations is similar.

First, we find the list of subscripts corresponding to the overarcs at the end of each arc of α\alpha:

The first row of the matrix gives the linking numbers of the null-homologous lift of ω1\omega_{1} with each lift of β\beta, and we see these numbers agree with the first column of the matrix of intersection numbers of 2-chains bounding lifts of β\beta with lifts of ω1\omega_{1}, confirming our first computation.

The algorithm also allows us to compute the linking numbers of each of the null-homologous pseudo-branch curves above (the three lifts of β\beta; the only null-homologous lift of ω1\omega_{1}; the single closed lift of ω2\omega_{2}) with each of the branch curves as well. These linking numbers are all zero, as one can also deduce from a geometric argument, using the construction in Cappell-Shaneson [9] together with the fact that the curves β\beta, ω1\omega_{1}, and ω2\omega_{2} lie on a Seifert surface for α\alpha.

6.3. The Python program

# Given an initial 3-cell and the color of a knot arc, returns the number of
# the 3-cell on the other side of the vertical 2-cell below the knot.
def wallcolorchange(oldcolor,wallcolor):
    if oldcolor==wallcolor:
        newcolor=oldcolor
    elif oldcolor != wallcolor:
        s=set()
        s.add(1)
        s.add(2)
        s.add(3)
        s.discard(oldcolor)
        s.discard(wallcolor)
        newcolor=s.pop()
    return newcolor

# A list of the 3-cells which contain each path-lift of a
# pseudo-branch curve.
def pseudolifts(subknotcolors,povernums,povertypes):
    l=len(povernums)
    lift1=[1]
    lift2=[2]
    lift3=[3]
    for i in range(0,l-1):
        if povertypes[i]==’k’:
            newcell1=wallcolorchange(lift1[i],subknotcolors[povernums[i]])
            lift1.append(newcell1)
            newcell2=wallcolorchange(lift2[i],subknotcolors[povernums[i]])
            lift2.append(newcell2)
            newcell3=wallcolorchange(lift3[i],subknotcolors[povernums[i]])
            lift3.append(newcell3)
        else:
            lift1.append(lift1[i])
            lift2.append(lift2[i])
            lift3.append(lift3[i])
    return lift1, lift2, lift3

# Returns the vector of values of the function w(i)
def subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums):
    l=len(subknottypes)
    if subknotcolors[0]==1:
        where=[2]
    else:
        where=[1]
    for j in range(0,l-1):
        if subknottypes[j]==’k’:
            where.append(wallcolorchange(where[j],
                subknotcolors[subknotovernums[j]]))
        elif subknottypes[j]==’p’:
            where.append(where[j])
    return where

# Returns the value of epsilon_1
def xingsign1(i,subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums):
    if subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums)[subknotovernums[i]]
                                                                 !=subknotcolors[i]:
        s=1
    else:
        s=-1
    return s

# Returns the value of epsilon_2
def xingsign2(i,subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums):
    if subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums)[i]
                                                 !=subknotcolors[subknotovernums[i]]:
        s=-1
    else:
        s=1
    return s

# Returns the value of epsilon_3
def xingsign3(i,subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums):
    if subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums)[i]
                        ==subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes,
ΨΨΨΨΨ    subknotovernums)[subknotovernums[i]]:
        s=-1
    else:
        s=1
    return s

# Returns the matrix A|-b, where a solution to Ax=b is the vector
# coefficients of the 2-cells A_2i in the chain bounding the index
# one branch curve
def br1surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors, subknottypes, subknotovernums, subknotsigns):
    n=len(subknotcolors)
    coefmatrix= [[0 for x in range(n+1)] for x in range(n)]

    for i in range(0,n):
        coefmatrix[i][i]+=1
        coefmatrix[i][(i+1)%n]-=1
        if subknottypes[i]==’k’ and subknotcolors[i]!=subknotcolors[subknotovernums[i]]:
                coefmatrix[i][subknotovernums[i]]+=xingsign1(i,subknotcolors,
                                                     subknottypes,subknotovernums)*
                                                   xingsign2(i,subknotcolors,
                                                     subknottypes,subknotovernums)
                coefmatrix[i][n]=-subknotsigns[i]*xingsign2(i, subknotcolors,
                                                     subknottypes,subknotovernums)
        elif subknottypes[i]==’k’ and subknotcolors[i]==subknotcolors[subknotovernums[i]]:
                coefmatrix[i][subknotovernums[i]]+= xingsign3(i,subknotcolors,
                                                   subknottypes,subknotovernums)*2
    return coefmatrix

# Returns the matrix A|-b, where a solution to Ax=b is the vector of
# coefficients of the 2-cells A_2i in the chain bounding the index
# two branch curve
def br2surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors, subknottypes, subknotovernums, subknotsigns):
    n=len(subknotcolors)
    coefmatrix=[[0 for x in range(n+1)] for x in range(n)]

    for i in range(0,n):
        coefmatrix[i][i]+=1
        coefmatrix[i][(i+1)%n]-=1
        if subknottypes[i]==’k’ and subknotcolors[i]!=
                                                subknotcolors[subknotovernums[i]]:
            coefmatrix[i][subknotovernums[i]]+=xingsign1(i,subknotcolors,
                                                 subknottypes,subknotovernums)*
                                               xingsign2(i,subknotcolors,
                                                 subknottypes,subknotovernums)
            coefmatrix[i][n]=xingsign2(i, subknotcolors,
                                                 subknottypes,subknotovernums)*.5*
                                               (subknotsigns[i]-xingsign1(i, subknotcolors,
                                                 subknottypes,subknotovernums))

        elif subknottypes[i]==’k’ and subknotcolors[i]==
                                                  subknotcolors[subknotovernums[i]]:
            coefmatrix[i][subknotovernums[i]]+= xingsign3(i,subknotcolors,
                                                  subknottypes,subknotovernums)*2
            coefmatrix[i][n]-=xingsign3(i, subknotcolors,
                                                  subknottypes,subknotovernums)
    return coefmatrix

# Finds a solution to the matrix equation Ax=b given the matrix A|-b
def solvefor2chain(matrixofcoefs, numcrossings):
    M=Matrix(matrixofcoefs)
    pivots=M.rref()[1]
    numpivots=len(pivots)
    RR=M.rref()[0]
    x=[0 for j in range(numcrossings)]

    if numcrossings in pivots:
        return ’False’

    else:
        for i in range(0,numpivots):
            x[pivots[i]]=-RR[i,numcrossings]

        return x

# Computes the intersection number of the 2nd pseudo-branch curve
# with the 2-chain bounded by the first pseudo-branch curve.
def p2intersectionwithp1surface(subknotcolors, subknotovernums,
    subknottypes, subknotsigns, p2overnums,p2overtypes, p2signs,
    p1overnums,p1signs,p1overtypes):

    total=[[0,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]
    l=len(p2overnums)
    p2lifts=pseudolifts(subknotcolors, p2overnums, p2overtypes)
    p1lifts=pseudolifts(subknotcolors,p1overnums,p1overtypes)
    coeflists=[]
    coeflists.append(solvefor2chain(p1surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors,subknottypes,
               subknotovernums,subknotsigns,p1signs,p1overnums,p1lifts[0]),
               len(subknotsigns)))
    coeflists.append(solvefor2chain(p1surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors,subknottypes,
               subknotovernums,subknotsigns,p1signs,p1overnums,p1lifts[1]),
               len(subknotsigns)))
    coeflists.append(solvefor2chain(p1surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors,subknottypes,
               subknotovernums,subknotsigns,p1signs,p1overnums,p1lifts[2]),
               len(subknotsigns)))
    where=subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes,subknotovernums)
    for s in range(0,3): # Three lifts of 1st pseudo-branch curve
        if coeflists[s]!=’False’:
            for i in range(0,l):# Arcs of the second pseudo-branch curve
                if p2overtypes[i]==’k’:
                    for j in range (0,3):
                        if p2lifts[j][i]==subknotcolors[p2overnums[i]]:
                            total[s][j]+=0
                        elif p2lifts[j][i]==where[p2overnums[i]]:
                            total[s][j]+=coeflists[s][p2overnums[i]]

                        elif p2lifts[j][i]!=where[p2overnums[i]]:
                            total[s][j]-=coeflists[s][p2overnums[i]]

                if p2overtypes[i]==’p’:
                    for j in range (0,3):
                        if p2lifts[j][i]!=p1lifts[s][p2overnums[i]]:
                            total[s][j]+=0

                        elif p2lifts[j][i]==p1lifts[s][p2overnums[i]]:
                            total[s][j]+=p2signs[i]

        else:
            total[s][0]=’x’
            total[s][1]=’x’
            total[s][2]=’x’

return total

#Compute the intersection number of the first pseudo-branch curve
# with the 2-chain bounded by the index 1 branch curve.
def p1intersectionwithbr1surface(subknotcolors, subknotovernums,
 subknottypes, subknotsigns, p1overnums, p1signs, p1overtypes):
    total=[0,0,0]
    l=len(p1overnums)
    p1lifts=pseudolifts(subknotcolors,p1overnums,p1overtypes)
    coeflist=solvefor2chain(br1surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors,
                      subknottypes,subknotovernums,subknotsigns),
                      len(subknotsigns))
    where=subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes, subknotovernums)
    if coeflist!=’False’:
        for i in range(0,l):
            if p1overtypes[i]==’k’:
                for j in range (0,3):
                    if p1lifts[j]==subknotcolors[p1overnums[i]]:
                        total[j]+=p1signs[i]
                    elif p1lifts[j]==where[p1overnums[i]]:
                        total[j]+=coeflist[p1overnums[i]]
                    elif p1lifts[j]!=where[p1overnums[i]]:
                        total[j]-=coeflist[p1overnums[i]]

    else:
        total=[’x’,’x’,’x’]
    return total

#Compute the intersection number of the first pseudo-branch curve
# with the 2-chain bounded by the index 2 branch curve.
def p1intersectionwithbr2surface(subknotcolors, subknotovernums, subknottypes,
                                 subknotsigns, p1overnums, p1signs, p1overtypes):
    total=[0,0,0]
    l=len(p1overnums)
    p1lifts=pseudolifts(subknotcolors,p1overnums,p1overtypes)
    coeflist=solvefor2chain(br2surfacecoefmatrix(subknotcolors,subknottypes,
             subknotovernums,subknotsigns),len(subknotsigns))
    where=subwhereisA2(subknotcolors,subknottypes, subknotovernums)
    if coeflist!=’False’:
        for i in range(0,l):
            if p1overtypes[i]==’k’:
                for j in range (0,3):
                    if p1lifts[j]==subknotcolors[p1overnums[i]]:
                        total[j]+=0
                    elif p1lifts[j]==where[p1overnums[i]]:
                        total[j]+=coeflist[p1overnums[i]]
                        if p1signs[i]==-1:
                             total[j]+=-1
                    elif p1lifts[j]!=where[p1overnums[i]]:
                        total[j]+=1-coeflist[p1overnums[i]]
                        if p1signs[i]==1:
                             total[j]+=1
    else:
        total=[’x’,’x’,’x’]
    return total
